scene.bubble: We're reading Great Expectations. Learn the third conditional and imagine how the past could have been different.
scene.intro: Our Grade 9 reading club has started Great Expectations by Charles Dickens — a story full of choices and regrets. In this unit you read about Pip, you learn the third conditional to imagine an unreal past and its results, and you talk about your own 'what if' questions. If you had made a different choice last year, where would you be now? Let's find out how to say it.

activities.title: Reading — the reading club on Great Expectations

data.title: Great Expectations: the choices that made Pip
data.author: sofia
data.text:
Our Grade 9 reading club has just started Great Expectations by Charles Dickens. It is the story of Pip, a poor boy who suddenly receives a fortune from a mysterious person and becomes a 'gentleman'.

At first, money changes Pip for the worse. He becomes proud and forgets the kind people who raised him. Later, he regrets it deeply. If he had stayed humble, he would not have hurt his old friends. If he had valued real friendship, he would have been happier.

In our discussion, Mateo made a good point. “If Pip hadn't become rich so easily,” he said, “he might have appreciated it more.” Nadia agreed: “If I had received a fortune at fifteen, I'm not sure I would have used it well either.”

That is the power of Dickens: he makes us ask 'what if?'. What if Pip had made different choices? The whole story would have changed. But if everything had gone perfectly, there would have been no lesson — and no novel.

By the end, Pip learns what really matters: kindness, honesty and gratitude. If only he had known that at the start!

data.title: Third conditional
data.intro: We use the third conditional to imagine a different past — something that did NOT happen — and its result. It is common when we talk about regrets.

examples.text: If Pip had stayed humble, he wouldn't have hurt his friends.
If I had known, I would have helped.
She might have won if she had trained more.

rules: Form: If + past perfect (had + participle), would have + participle.
It describes an unreal past — the opposite of what really happened.
Use might have / could have for a possible (not certain) past result.

items.sentence: If Pip had been wiser, he ___ his friends.
If I ___ earlier, I would have caught the bus.
She would have passed if she ___ harder.
We ___ won if we had trained more.
If they had listened, this ___ happened.

data.script: Good morning, Grade 9. Let's talk about Great Expectations. Remember, this is Pip's story: a poor boy who suddenly becomes rich. Our big question is about choices. If Pip had stayed in the village, his life would have been very different. For Wednesday, prepare one 'what if' question about the story. Also, Sofía has volunteered to lead the discussion, and Mateo will bring the film version. See you then!

data.instructions: Choose the correct answer to complete each sentence, like in the B1 Preliminary exam.

items.sentence: If we had left earlier, we ___ the train.
She ___ have passed if she had revised.

activities.title: Speaking — imagine the past. In pairs, then record it.

data.text: In pairs, talk about the past using the third conditional. Model: “What would you have done if you had won a fortune at fifteen?” — “If I had won a fortune, I would have travelled the world.” 1) What would you have done if you had been born in another country? 2) Is there a choice you would have made differently? 3) What would have happened if you hadn't come to this school? Then record your best answers.

homework.prompt: Write a short reflection (6–8 sentences) about Pip, or about a 'what if' in your own life, using the third conditional. Example: 'If Pip had stayed humble, he would not have lost his friends.' Use at least three third conditionals. Capital letters and full stops!
